content: Uterine prolapse refers to the descent or displacement of the uterus from its normal anatomical position in the pelvic cavity into the vaginal canal. Symptoms of Uterine Prolapse: Patients may experience a sensation as though they are sitting on a small ball. Sexual intercourse may become difficult or painful. There may be frequent urination or a sudden, urgent need to empty the bladder. A dull ache or discomfort in the lower back is common. Pain during sexual intercourse is frequently reported. The uterus and cervix may visibly protrude through the vaginal opening. Recurrent bladder infections can occur. A sensation of heaviness or pulling in the pelvic region is often described. Vaginal bleeding or an increase in vaginal discharge may be present. Symptoms tend to worsen when standing or sitting for prolonged periods. Causes of Uterine Prolapse: The uterus is supported in the pelvis by muscles, ligaments, and connective tissues. Uterine prolapse occurs when these supportive structures weaken, allowing the uterus to descend into the vaginal canal. Risk Factors: Women who have had one or more vaginal deliveries are at higher risk. Aging and the decline in estrogen levels after menopause contribute to the weakening of pelvic support structures. Although rare, a pelvic tumor can also lead to uterine prolapse. Chronic constipation and the associated straining can worsen the condition. When to Seek Medical Attention: Patients should schedule an appointment with their healthcare provider if they experience symptoms suggestive of uterine prolapse. Diagnosis: A pelvic examination is performed, often while the patient is asked to bear down as if pushing. This helps assess the extent of uterine descent. Mild prolapse is characterized by the cervix descending into the lower part of the vagina. Moderate prolapse occurs when the cervix protrudes through the vaginal opening. The examination may also reveal associated conditions, such as a cystocele (bladder bulging into the vaginal wall) or a rectocele (rectum bulging into the vaginal wall). The urethra and bladder may be found to have shifted to a lower position in the pelvis. In rare cases, a pelvic tumor causing the prolapse may be detected during the examination. Treatment Options: Treatment is not always necessary unless symptoms are bothersome. Most women seek treatment when the uterus descends to the vaginal opening. Treatment options include the use of a vaginal pessary, lifestyle modifications, or surgery. Vaginal Pessary: A vaginal pessary is a device, often donut-shaped and made of rubber or plastic, that is inserted into the vagina to support the uterus. It can be used as a temporary or permanent solution. Pessaries are custom-fitted for each patient, and some resemble a diaphragm used for contraception. Many women can be taught to insert, clean, and remove the pessary themselves. Potential side effects include irritation of the vaginal walls, abnormal-smelling discharge, and, in some cases, damage to the vaginal tissue. Some pessaries may interfere with sexual intercourse by limiting the depth of penetration. Lifestyle Changes: Weight loss is recommended for obese women with uterine prolapse. Avoiding heavy lifting and straining is advised, as these activities can worsen symptoms. Chronic coughing should be managed, and smoking cessation is recommended if the cough is related to smoking. Surgery: Surgery is considered when symptoms become more severe than the risks associated with the procedure. The choice of surgical intervention depends on factors such as the degree of prolapse, the patient’s desire for future pregnancies, other medical conditions, the patient’s age and general health, and the desire to preserve vaginal function. Some procedures, such as sacrospinous fixation, involve using nearby ligaments to support the uterus without removing it. A vaginal hysterectomy is often performed to correct uterine prolapse. Any associated sagging of the vaginal walls, urethra, bladder, or rectum can be addressed surgically during the same procedure. Prognosis: Women with mild uterine prolapse often do not experience significant symptoms and may not require treatment. Vaginal pessaries are effective for many women. Surgical treatment generally yields excellent results, although some women may require additional treatment in the future. Possible Complications: Severe uterine prolapse can lead to ulceration and infection of the cervix and vaginal walls. Urinary tract infections and other urinary symptoms may occur due to a cystocele. Constipation and hemorrhoids may develop as a result of a rectocele. Prevention: Performing Kegel exercises to strengthen the pelvic floor muscles can reduce the risk of uterine prolapse. Postmenopausal women may benefit from estrogen therapy, either vaginally or orally, to maintain the tone of connective tissues and muscles.
